title: James Gorman, Chairman and CEO, Morgan Stanley
description: Full story: http://insights.som.yale.edu/insights/what-does-it-take-survive-wall-street  WHAT DOES IT TAKE TO SURVIVE ON WALL STREET? Any financial institution that is going to last for decades will have to survive a crisis or two—most likely by adapting and innovating, perhaps by leaving behind chunks of its old identity. Yale Insights spoke with James Gorman, chairman and CEO of Morgan Stanley, one of two major investment banks to survive the 2008 financial crisis, about how the firm has managed to refashion itself and prepare for the future.

asr.full_text: I think you are in the right place. So, I thank you for your time this morning and with all this information, I would like to thank you for being here today. We hope to continue and we are very much in agreement that this program has the potential to evolve within the next five years as well. But that is just the beginning because it is not at this moment that we have done quite a job. I would like to say thanks to every one of our presenters for So I sure hope it's not going to continue for the next five years at this pace. But we came out of probably the largest financial crisis since the depression and arguably for financial institutions even prior to that. So what the firm has done in first becoming a bank holding company, second, acquiring a very large wealth manager to now be one of the largest two or three wealth managers globally. Thirdly, to shut all of our proprietary trading businesses and our hedge fund businesses and refocus on our client activities. Fourthly to bring down our leverage from 35 times to 12 times and double our capital. These are once in a decade changes. Any individual one of these, and we did five or six of them over a four or five year period. I think the major strategic changes have taken place, I would be surprised if there are major strategic changes for us over the next several years, but clearly in the new regulatory environment we are continuing to refine our business model to generate for our shareholders the kinds of returns they expect in an environment where we're using much more capital to prosecute the businesses that we're doing for our clients. So it's more a question of now that we've got the new business model, lets make it work. Let's deliver performance above our cost of capital which we and most of our industry are not doing at this point. The major factors that are going to drive changes, absorbing the new regulatory regimes globally? The US is, I would argue, ahead of where Europe is certainly is in making regulatory changes. We need to now harmonize those changes because we're a global entity, we're U.S. headquartered, we're not a U.S. entity. We're a global entity. So harmonise the regulatory changes and adapt your business model accordingly. We need to feed the businesses that get generous returns on capital, starve the businesses that don't. Realign our resources like that, and most importantly, and particularly to a school like Yale is recognising we're in the war for talent still. We succeed because we attract very very high quality dedicated professionals to our business who have a real passion for being in the banking business. There are a lot of opportunities for growth. At a macro level with the global economic recovery that is taking place, clearly the financial sector tends to recover faster than most industries, and within the financial sector the securities subsector recovers fast. So, in terms of being positioned for global economic growth, we're clearly positioned for that. Secondly, if you look at some of the regions of the world world we sold 22% of Morgan Stanley to the largest bank in Japan Mitsubishi, UFJ and we have a wonderful partnership with them and with the surge that's taking place the reinvigoration of the Japanese economy that's a wonderful platform for us to find growth and thirdly just across our various businesses we've we were so distracted in the last few years trying to adapt our business model to the new reality it'll be kind of fun just getting back to focusing all of our energies on serving our clients I think a lot of our competitors globally is still focused on changing their business models post crisis we've done that we've got that behind us so we're going to be focusing all of our energy on doing business. The emerging markets are always by definition fragile because they're emerging they haven't emerged and are not developed market so you're going to see more volatility. That said, I get excited about Brazil. I get excited about Indonesia- where we have set said I get excited about Brazil. I get excited about Indonesia where we've set up an equities trading business. I certainly think that China over the next several years under the new leadership of Xi Jinping should perform at 7 plus percent GDP growth which makes it a very attractive market. So there are huge pockets of opportunity but they're going to be speed bumps as we adjust whether it's pulling liquidity out of the system as tapering of the Federal Reserve quantitative easing occurs whether it's some of the political turmoil we're seeing in in a number of countries around the world all. All of those factors affect domestic economic growth.
